item.title: Karatsu Morning Market — Guide
item.description: Karatsu’s morning market is a small, friendly street market that brings the everyday life of this castle and fishing town to life in the early hours. Local vendors — many of them older women from the surrounding area and coast — line the street with their stalls, selling the freshest catch from the Genkai Sea, seasonal vegetables and fruit, homemade pickles, dried fish and seaweed, and local specialties, often straight from their own boats and farms.

item.title: Yobuko: The Squid Fishing Village — Guide
item.description: Yobuko, a small fishing port on Saga’s northern Genkai Sea coast near Karatsu, is famous throughout Japan for one thing above all: its squid. The waters here yield superb squid, and Yobuko’s signature dish is ika no ikizukuri — ‘live squid’ sashimi, served so fresh that the flesh is still translucent and glistening, sliced while the squid is barely out of the tank and prized for its clean sweetness and crunchy texture.

item.title: Hachinohe Morning Market: Japan's Largest Sunday Market — Guide
item.description: The Tatehana Wharf morning market in Hachinohe is one of Japan’s largest — over 300 stalls line the wharf from around 3am each Sunday (spring–autumn), selling fresh seafood, grilled fish, local snacks and handmade goods. Fishermen and farmers trade directly with the public in a wholly local, un-touristy atmosphere. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe, Aomori (Tatehana Wharf) Hours Sun ~3:00–9:00 (Mar–Dec) Admission Free; pay per stall Time needed 1–2 hours Best time Sunday mornings, Mar–Dec What to Try 300+ stalls of seafood, produce and street food.

item.title: Hakodate Guide: Night View, Morning Market & Access
item.description: A historic port at Hokkaido’s southern tip, Hakodate was one of Japan’s first cities opened to foreign trade, and it wears that heritage beautifully. The headline attraction is the night view from Mt. Hakodate — the glittering, hourglass-shaped cityscape pinched between two bays, rated among Japan’s finest. By day, dig into the bustling morning market for the freshest crab, uni and squid-on-rice, wander the European-flavoured Motomachi slopes, and admire the star-shaped Goryokaku fort.

item.title: Hokkaido Seafood Guide: Crab, Uni, Kaisendon & Where to Eat
item.description: Cold, rich northern seas make Hokkaido a paradise for seafood — arguably the best in Japan. This is the place to feast on sweet king and snow crab, melt-in-the-mouth sea urchin (uni), glistening salmon roe (ikura), plump scallops and the freshest sashimi. The signature way to enjoy it all is a kaisendon — a bowl of rice heaped with a rainbow of raw seafood — devoured at a bustling morning market.

item.title: Katsuura Morning Market & Sashimi Guide: What to Eat & Access
item.description: The fishing town of Katsuura on the Boso coast is a paradise for seafood lovers, home to one of Japan’s three great morning markets — a tradition running for over 400 years. Each morning, stalls along the old streets brim with the night’s catch, vegetables and pickles, and nearby diners serve glistening sashimi rice bowls and set meals built around the day’s freshest fish straight off the boats. Katsuura is also the surprising birthplace of fiery Katsuura tantanmen, a local spicy ramen.

item.title: Tsukiji Outer Market Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Food Morning
item.description: For 83 years, Tsukiji was the largest fish market on Earth — the beating heart of Tokyo’s relationship with seafood, where billions of yen of tuna changed hands before dawn. In 2018 the famous wholesale auctions moved to a modern facility in Toyosu, but here’s what most visitors don’t realise: the part you actually want to visit never left. The bustling Outer Market (Tsukiji Jogai Shijo) — the warren of stalls, knife shops, and tiny restaurants where the public eats — is still right where it always was, still serving some of the freshest, most exciting food in Tokyo, every morning.
